Here’s a thorough summary of the **2011–12 Harvard Crimson men’s basketball team**, one of the most important teams in Harvard basketball history.

## Quick overview

- **School:** Harvard University
- **Season:** 2011–12 NCAA Division I men’s basketball
- **Conference:** Ivy League
- **Head coach:** **Tommy Amaker** (5th season)
- **Home court:** **Lavietes Pavilion** in Cambridge, Massachusetts
- **Overall record:** **26–5**
- **Ivy League record:** **12–2**
- **Finish:** **Ivy League champion**
- **NCAA tournament:** Lost in the NCAA tournament to **Vanderbilt**, 79–70

This team is most remembered for delivering **Harvard’s first outright Ivy League championship** and the program’s **first NCAA tournament berth since 1946**.

---

## Why this team mattered

The 2011–12 season was a landmark year for Harvard basketball.

### 1. First outright Ivy League title
Harvard had shared the Ivy title the year before, but in 2011–12 it **won the league outright**, which was a major breakthrough.

### 2. First NCAA tournament bid in decades
Harvard had not appeared in the NCAA tournament since **1946**, so this team ended a **66-year drought**.

### 3. National relevance
This was the season when Harvard basketball moved from being a good Ivy program to a **nationally noticed team**. The team spent time in the **national rankings**, which was a huge deal for the program.

### 4. Program-building moment under Tommy Amaker
Tommy Amaker had been steadily rebuilding Harvard, and this season was the clearest proof that the program had become a real contender, not just within the Ivy League but nationally.

---

## Season performance

### Overall record: 26–5
Harvard won **26 games**, which was among the best seasons in school history at the time.

### Ivy League play: 12–2
The Crimson went **12–2** in conference play and captured the league title.

### NCAA tournament
Harvard earned the Ivy League’s automatic bid and entered the NCAA tournament, where it lost to **Vanderbilt** in the round of 64 (then officially called the “second round” because of the First Four structure).

---

## Style and identity of the team

This Harvard team was known for:

- **Strong defense**
- **Discipline**
- **Half-court execution**
- **Maturity and experience**
- **Balanced scoring**
- **Physical interior play**

Tommy Amaker’s teams often emphasized defense, rebounding, and smart decision-making, and that was very true of the 2011–12 group. They were not just winning because they were in the Ivy League; they were beating strong nonconference teams too.

---

## Key players

### Keith Wright
The biggest star on the team.

- Senior forward/center
- Team leader
- Go-to inside scorer
- One of the best players in the Ivy League

Wright was the emotional and basketball centerpiece of the team. He was named **Ivy League Player of the Year** and was crucial to Harvard’s title run. He brought scoring, rebounding, experience, and toughness.

### Kyle Casey
A very important frontcourt player.

- Athletic forward
- Strong rebounder and finisher
- Major two-way contributor

Casey gave Harvard another physical presence up front and helped make the team hard to handle around the basket.

### Brandyn Curry
A key backcourt piece.

- Point guard
- Floor leader
- Important defender and playmaker

Curry helped organize the offense and brought steadiness to the backcourt.

### Laurent Rivard
One of the team’s best perimeter threats.

- Guard
- Excellent shooter
- Stretch option who helped space the floor

Rivard gave Harvard an outside shooting dimension that balanced its interior attack.

### Oliver McNally
A veteran contributor.

- Guard
- Experienced leader
- Important part of the rotation

McNally added leadership and reliability.

### Steve Moundou-Missi
A younger frontcourt contributor.

- Forward
- Athletic and energetic
- Helped with rebounding and defense

He would become more important in later years, but he already offered useful depth and athleticism.

### Christian Webster, Corbin Miller, Kenyatta Smith
These players also helped fill out the rotation and contributed to the team’s overall depth, especially on defense and on the perimeter.

---

## Coaching

### Tommy Amaker
This season was one of the signature achievements of **Tommy Amaker’s** career.

Before Harvard, Amaker had coached at Seton Hall and Michigan. At Harvard, he took on a difficult job:

- recruiting high-level players to an academically demanding school,
- trying to build a winner in a place with limited basketball tradition compared with major powers,
- and elevating the program in a league where every game matters because the Ivy League did not have a conference tournament at the time.

By 2011–12, the rebuild had clearly worked.

Amaker’s impact included:

- improved recruiting,
- stronger defensive identity,
- greater national visibility,
- and raising expectations for Harvard basketball permanently.

---

## Notable achievements and milestones

Some of the biggest accomplishments associated with this team:

- **Won Harvard’s first outright Ivy League championship**
- **Reached Harvard’s first NCAA tournament since 1946**
- **Set or matched school-level success benchmarks for wins**
- **Earned national ranking attention**
- Helped establish Harvard as a legitimate mid-major/national story

This was not just a good season by Harvard standards. It was one of the defining seasons in the history of Ivy League basketball in that era.

---

## National ranking significance

The 2011–12 team was notable for helping Harvard gain unusual national attention for an Ivy League program.

They were ranked in the **AP Top 25**, a major milestone for the school. Harvard had essentially never been thought of in modern times as a nationally ranked basketball program, so this mattered symbolically as much as competitively.

It showed that the program’s rise was not just an East Coast academic-sports curiosity; it was being taken seriously by voters and media nationally.

---

## Nonconference success

One reason the team got so much attention was that it did not pad its record only against league opponents. It earned respect through **quality nonconference wins**, including a headline-making road win over a highly ranked **Florida State** team.

That result was one of the biggest regular-season wins in school history and helped announce Harvard as a team worth watching nationally.

Harvard also played a challenging enough schedule to make people believe the record was real.

---

## Ivy League race

In the Ivy League, every regular-season game mattered enormously because there was **no Ivy League tournament** at the time. The regular-season champion got the NCAA bid.

That meant Harvard’s march to the title carried constant pressure. There was no second chance.

By going **12–2**, the Crimson separated itself from the league and secured the automatic tournament berth.

This also mattered because Harvard had come painfully close before. The previous season, Harvard had shared the Ivy title but did not make the NCAA tournament after losing a playoff to Princeton. So the 2011–12 team finished the job.

---

## NCAA tournament game vs. Vanderbilt

Harvard entered the NCAA tournament with a lot of excitement around the program. In its tournament game, it faced **Vanderbilt** of the SEC.

- **Result:** Vanderbilt 79, Harvard 70

Harvard lost, but the appearance itself was historic. The team was competitive and showed that the program belonged on that stage, even if it did not yet break through for a tournament win.

That breakthrough would come later under Amaker, but this team laid the groundwork.

---

## Legacy

The 2011–12 team’s legacy is huge.

### It changed Harvard basketball
This team turned Harvard from a program with occasional promise into one with **sustained expectations**.

### It paved the way for later teams
Later Harvard teams would:
- return to the NCAA tournament,
- win NCAA tournament games,
- and become the dominant Ivy program for stretches.

The 2011–12 team was the bridge between “improving program” and “proven winner.”

### It is one of the best teams in school history
For many fans and historians, this is one of the most important Harvard basketball teams ever, if not the most important, because of:
- the outright Ivy title,
- the NCAA bid,
- the national ranking,
- and the long-term impact on the program.

---

## Commonly remembered names from the team

The names most associated with the 2011–12 Harvard team are:

- **Tommy Amaker**
- **Keith Wright**
- **Kyle Casey**
- **Brandyn Curry**
- **Laurent Rivard**
- **Oliver McNally**
- **Steve Moundou-Missi**

---

## Short summary

If you want the shortest possible description:

> The 2011–12 Harvard Crimson men’s basketball team, coached by Tommy Amaker, went 26–5 and 12–2 in the Ivy League, won Harvard’s first outright Ivy League title, earned the school’s first NCAA tournament bid since 1946, spent time nationally ranked, and became one of the foundational teams in the rise of modern Harvard basketball.

If you want, I can also give you:
1. a **game-by-game season summary**,  
2. the **full roster and stats**, or  
3. a **comparison with the 2010–11 and 2012–13 Harvard teams**.
